British Journal of Educational Technolog.title: From emotion regulation to academic success: A self‐determination theory‐based emotional agent‐mediated approach
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Emotion regulation has been recognized as a key factor affecting students' academic success. However, in conventional school settings, it is challenging to foster students' emotion regulation owing to the involvement of complex factors that might influence students' conscious and unconscious behaviours. To address this issue, a self‐determination theory (SDT)‐based emotional agent framework was proposed, and an emotional agent (EmoAgent), capable of proactively detecting students' emotional states and providing emotional regulation strategies to individual students in addition to the provision of conventional learning supports, was implemented. To assess the effectiveness of the proposed approach, an 8‐week quasi‐experiment was designed with 173 sixth graders from four classes taking the Information Technology course in a primary school. Two classes (87 students) comprised the experimental group (EG) which used the SDT‐based emotional agent‐mediated (SDT‐EA) approach, while the other two classes (86 students) comprised the control group (CG) which learned with the SDT‐based conventional agent (STD‐CA), which is capable of providing learning supports but without considering emotional factors. The experimental results showed that (1) the SDT‐EA approach significantly outperformed the SDT‐CA approach in academic achievement; (2) the SDT‐EA approach engaged students in positive emotional experiences, whereas the SDT‐CA approach exposed students to more negative emotional experiences; (3) negative emotion was significantly negatively associated with academic achievement, moderated by the SDT‐EA approach.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic?
                          
                            
                              Within self‐determination theory, if the three psychological needs of autonomy, competence and relatedness are met, students’ intrinsic motivation is activated and in turn their academic emotion is regulated, which shapes their well‐being, engagement and academic success.
                            
                            
                              GenAI–human collaboration can facilitate students’ self‐determined and personalized learning.
                            
                            
                              Most pedagogical agents tend to assist with personalized cognitive support rather than with emotion regulation or emotional support.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What does this paper add?
                          
                            
                              Merging affective computing technology with GenAI, this study constructed an emotional agent with emotion sensing, recognition, feedback and regulation, providing emotional and cognitive supports.
                            
                            
                              Using process mining techniques, this study found that the emotional agent facilitated students’ emotion regulation from negative to positive.
                            
                            
                              The emotional agent moderated the effect of negative emotions on academic success.
                            
                            
                              The emotional agent can significantly promote academic achievement.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              The study findings imply that the SDT‐based emotional agent‐mediated approach shows promise for strengthening students’ self‐regulated learning.
                            
                            
                              The study offers a viable model for integrating socio‐emotional learning with subject‐matter instruction.
                            
                            
                              The SDT‐based emotional agent can be embedded in regular instruction to instantiate a self‐determined learning paradigm.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Effects of
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    chatbot‐supported cooperative flipped classroom on student collaboration, self‐regulated learning and academic performance: A mastery learning perspective
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Despite the increasing application of AI chatbots, few studies have examined the effectiveness of AI chatbot‐supported cooperative‐flipped classrooms in university teaching. Based on mastery learning theory, this study employed a quasi‑experimental design to examine how an AI chatbot‐supported cooperative‑flipped classroom influences students' collaboration, self‐regulated learning and academic performance, and whether students with different prior knowledge levels demonstrate distinct patterns under AI‐supported flipped learning. This study involved 154 junior students from a normal university, including an experimental group (
                    n
                     = 87) and a control group (
                    n
                     = 67), who were taught by the same instructor over an 11‐week period. Quantitative data from pretest and posttest scores and self‑report scales were analysed using
                    t
                    ‐tests and ANCOVA, whereas qualitative interview data from 10 experimental group students were analysed using Epistemic Network Analysis to compare collaboration and self‑regulated learning patterns across prior knowledge groups. The results showed that, compared to the control group, the experimental group demonstrated significantly higher posttest scores in collaboration, self‐regulated learning and academic performance. Within the experimental group, students with higher levels of AI chatbot interaction also significantly outperformed those with lower interaction levels in academic performance. Further, Epistemic Network Analysis results revealed that in AI chatbot‑supported flipped learning, students with lower prior knowledge exhibited denser collaboration networks, requiring more cognitive input and more frequent dimension switching to coordinate collaborative processes. In contrast, students with higher prior knowledge demonstrated stronger connections between the seeking, engaging and reflecting dimensions in their self‐regulated learning networks, reflecting more integrated self‐regulatory behaviour. This study provides empirical support for mastery learning theory and demonstrates the effectiveness of AI chatbot‐supported cooperative‐flipped classrooms, offering implications for differentiated teaching based on students' prior knowledge levels.
                  
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            
                              Flipped classrooms are associated with improvements in students' self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic performance compared with traditional instruction.
                            
                            
                              Group cooperation during pre‐class activities can enhance peer interaction and collaboration, but is often constrained by uneven participation and limited instructional support.
                            
                            
                              AI chatbots have been applied as learning assistants in higher education to provide feedback and learning resources, yet their role in structured pre‐class group cooperation remains insufficiently examined.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            
                              AI chatbot‐supported cooperative‐flipped classrooms significantly enhance students' collaboration, self‐regulated learning and academic performance compared with traditional group‐based flipped learning.
                            
                            
                              Epistemic network analysis shows that students with different levels of prior knowledge exhibit distinct collaboration and self‐regulation patterns when supported by an AI chatbot.
                            
                            
                              The findings demonstrate that AI chatbots can function as mastery‐oriented scaffolds by guiding task division, clarifying learning goals and supporting feedback during pre‐class group discussions, thereby strengthening students' readiness for subsequent in‐class learning.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and/or policy
                        
                          
                            
                              Practitioners are encouraged to integrate AI chatbots into pre‐class group discussions to provide structured guidance, timely feedback and support for collaborative knowledge construction.
                            
                            
                              Instructional support should be differentiated by prior knowledge: learners with lower prior knowledge benefit from clearer goals and stronger cognitive scaffolding, whereas higher‐achieving learners benefit from tasks emphasizing integration, reflection and assessment.
                            
                            
                              For large‐scale or resource‐constrained teaching contexts, AI chatbot‐supported cooperative‐flipped classrooms offer a scalable approach to implementing mastery learning and differentiated instruction in technology‐enhanced pedagogy.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title: Not all collaboration benefits from competition: Collaboration modes in a computational thinking game
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Digital game‐based learning often leverages social dynamics to enhance engagement, yet the interplay between collaborative structures and competitive pressures remains complex. This study investigated different collaboration modes and how they interact with competition to influence computational thinking (CT) learning, group metacognition and in‐game behaviours. Adopting a quasi‐experimental approach with a 3 × 2 factorial design, 148 seventh‐grade students were recruited via purposive sampling from intact classes. Participants played the game in pairs, with or without competition, in one of three collaboration modes: paired gaming on one computer, collaboration on respective computers with turn‐taking or cooperation on respective computers with role assignment. Data were analysed using quantitative methods to assess learning outcomes and behavioural sequence analysis to identify interaction patterns. Results revealed significant main effects of collaboration mode and an interaction effect between collaboration and competition. The cooperative group with competition achieved the highest CT outcomes, and the paired gaming group with competition reported the highest level of group metacognition. In contrast, the collaborative group with competition had the lowest level of learning outcomes and group metacognition. Behavioural sequence analyses identified unique patterns that corroborate the quantitative findings. Notably, competition undermined the collaborative turn‐taking mode while enhancing cooperative and paired gaming modes, highlighting the need to carefully match collaboration structures with competitive elements in designing game‐based learning.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Collaboration and competition are widely used in digital game‐based learning (DGBL) to enhance engagement, motivation and problem‐solving.
                            
                            
                              Prior studies have often examined collaboration and competition separately, leaving the interactive effects between these social dynamics on computational thinking (CT) and group metacognition underexplored.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              Different collaboration modes significantly shaped CT learning and group metacognition.
                            
                            
                              Competition alone showed no benefits for CT learning or group metacognition.
                            
                            
                              Cooperative + competition fostered clear roles, strategic play and higher CT.
                            
                            
                              Competition weakened collaboration learning's CT performance and led to fragmented behaviours.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and policy
                          
                            
                              Carefully match collaboration structures with competition features when designing game‐based or group learning activities.
                            
                            
                              Use competition selectively—beneficial in cooperative tasks with clear role assignments, but potentially detrimental in open collaboration requiring trust and mutual regulation.
                            
                            
                              Integrate competitive and collaborative elements intentionally rather than additively.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Academics’ (Re) construction of teacher identities in the context of technology integration at a South African university
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  Integrating technology into higher education teaching is reshaping pedagogical practices and prompting academics to (re)construct their professional identities. This qualitative case study explores how academics at a South African university respond to these changes, drawing on identity theory and the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) model to analyse the data. Data were collected from 12 purposively selected academics through semi-structured interviews and were analysed thematically. Findings indicate that academics are compelled to transition from traditional to interactive, student-centred teaching, requiring ongoing adaptation to emerging digital tools, multimedia integration, and data analytics for student monitoring. However, this shift also introduced identity tensions driven by increased workload, student disengagement, and recurring technical issues. Despite these challenges, the participants reported enhanced pedagogical effectiveness and renewed engagement through digital methods. The study highlights the dual nature of technology integration as both a disruptor and an enabler of professional growth and argues for comprehensive institutional support structures, including professional development and technical assistance. The findings contribute to the discourse on teacher identity in digitally evolving higher education environments and offer practical implications for policies and professional learning.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: The influence of socratic dialogue within GenAI on critical thinking and technology perception
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  The increasing accessibility of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Generative AI (GenAI) and chatbots, highlights the need for users to develop critical thinking skills to evaluate information and understand these systems. While critical thinking is essential for interacting with such technologies, current AI literacy efforts lack robust empirical validation, and effective educational methodologies have yet to be explored. This study explores the potential of the Socratic Method, a structured dialogue-based approach that fosters reflection and critical questioning, to support the development of critical thinking within a GenAI environment. Recognizing that many technology-enhanced and Socratic learning environments often overlook the role of learners’ domain expertise and prior knowledge in shaping effective questioning strategies, the study further compares within-domain and outside-domain Socratic dialogues to evaluate the pedagogical effectiveness of both conditions. Eighty participants, comprising higher education students and teachers, took part in workshops where they interacted with GenAI using two Socratic-style prompts, one within-domain and one outside-domain, and completed questionnaires assessing critical thinking, technical competence, and trust in technology after each interaction. Findings highlight the value of guiding GenAI interactions through Socratic reasoning within domain-relevant contexts to enhance perceived critical thinking, while also stressing the challenges of influencing user trust and perceived competence in technology.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Instructors’ perceptions of a large language model framework for generating automated multiple-choice questions from video transcripts
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  Video-Based Learning has become a central modality in digital education, with embedded Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs) recognized as an effective strategy for promoting engagement and assessing comprehension. However, manually creating high-quality MCQs is challenging for instructors. This study presents a framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLM) to automate MCQ generation from video transcripts while ensuring alignment with established item-writing criteria. Unlike most prior approaches, the framework explicitly integrates the Item-Writing Flaws (IWF) checklist into the generation prompt, rather than using it solely for post-hoc evaluation. It segments video transcripts into topics, extracts and classifies key concepts, and applies structured prompting strategies to generate MCQs adhering to the IWF checklist and additional criteria from the literature, including relevance, difficulty, contextual specificity, and answerability. The framework was evaluated through a mixed-methods study involving seven instructors from diverse disciplines who assessed 257 generated MCQs. The results indicate that the majority of items met established quality guidelines. Specifically, 84.05% of the questions were rated as clear, 86.38% contained plausible distractors, and 93.39% were directly answerable based on the video content. The main issues identified concerned relevance, reflecting occasional difficulty in distinguishing illustrative examples from core instructional content, and linguistic precision, with a tendency to overgeneralize instructors’ statements. In semi-structured interviews, instructors reported that the framework could substantially reduce MCQ preparation time while requiring only minor refinements to improve question specificity. Overall, the findings suggest that embedding pedagogical quality principles directly into LLM prompting represents a viable and promising direction for assessment automation.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: Beyond Content Digitization: A Smart Contract‐Based Solution for Ownership and Motivation in Online Learning (Course‐Chain)
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Introduction
                    With the advancement of the digital age, traditional face‐to‐face education and training programs have been increasingly replaced by online courses, which consist of live digital lectures and pre‐recorded video content. However, although online course platforms have succeeded in digitizing the essential requirements of traditional ones, they remain insufficient in areas such as ownership declaration and the resale of courses.
                  
                  
                    Aim
                    This study aims to investigate the feasibility of a blockchain‐based online learning platform that integrates Non‐Fungible Tokens (NFTs), smart contracts, cryptocurrency payments, and InterPlanetary File System (IPFS). The proposed Course‐Chain platform is developed and evaluated to assess its architecture, core functionalities, secondary‐market mechanisms, decentralized certification process, and transaction‐cost characteristics. In addition, the study explores how blockchain‐based ownership, transparent transactions, and decentralized credential management can improve access to educational resources, support learner engagement, and foster a more trustworthy online learning environment.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    The developed Course‐Chain platform offers features that enable second‐hand course sales, ensure transparency, support decentralization, and protect user data. To achieve this, the platform integrates Blockchain, NFTs, Cryptocurrency, IPFS, and Digital Wallet technologies in a unified manner. Within the proposed platform, a set of smart contracts was implemented using Solidity. Through the developed platform, students are provided with greater opportunities to try out courses, while new solutions have been proposed to enhance user trust by ensuring data security.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    On the Ethereum blockchain network, the total gas consumption for all transactions executed on the platform amounted to 722,768. The study's results demonstrate that the proposed IPFS‐based and blockchain‐based system operates successfully and remains open to future enhancements.
                  
                  
                    Discussion
                    Grounded in the research questions, the findings demonstrate that NFT‐based course ownership and secondary‐market transactions are technically feasible using ERC‐721 standards and smart contracts, enabling a configurable, creator‐defined resale mechanism. Regarding transaction costs, Layer‐2 solutions (Polygon) are shown to significantly enhance the economic viability of the architecture compared to the high‐fee Ethereum network. Furthermore, non‐transferable NFT credentials, combined with IPFS storage, effectively mitigate the risks of forgery and data loss while preserving user privacy. Despite the technical success, key limitations of the platform include the relatively high gas fees on the Ethereum network, the user learning curve associated with Web3 wallet management, and the lack of empirical validation regarding its pedagogical effects.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    The primary objective of this study was to address the shortcomings of existing platforms by providing a more reliable, transparent, decentralized, and potentially motivating experience for both users and course creators. The results demonstrate the technical feasibility of the proposed architecture. It was also found that the proposed platform, due to its Ethereum‐based design, incurs relatively high gas fees. Therefore, migrating to the Polygon network has been considered for future developments, as empirical results indicate that such a transition would significantly reduce gas costs. Unlike prior decentralized education platforms, Course‐Chain contributes a configurable, creator‐defined framework combining optional resale restriction, supply control, and programmable royalties. That enables a flexible and regulated secondary market for course ownership.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: The Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Learning Outcomes in Higher Education: A Meta‐Analysis
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    In recent years, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has been increasingly adopted in higher education to support undergraduate learning. Despite its rapid integration into educational settings, the effects of GenAI on learning outcomes remain inconclusive owing to varying study designs and outcome measures.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study aims to synthesise empirical evidence on the effectiveness of GenAI in improving undergraduate students' learning outcomes across three dimensions: academic performance, professional skills and emotional attitude.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    A meta‐analysis was conducted on 35 experimental and quasi‐experimental studies published between 2022 and 2024, retrieved from Web of Science (SCI‐Expanded and SSCI), EBSCO (ERIC) and Scopus databases. The analysis examined the overall effects of GenAI and explored the moderating variables, including discipline type, teaching model, intervention duration, learning method and GenAI interaction method.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    
                      We test the impact of GenAI on undergraduate learning outcomes across three dimensions: academic performance, professional skills and emotional attitude. The findings reveal that: (1) GenAI significantly improves students' learning outcomes, with a particularly prominent positive effect on professional skills (
                      g
                       = 0.72) and moderate positive effects on academic performance (
                      g
                       = 0.46) and emotional attitude (
                      g
                       = 0.44). (2) The effects of GenAI are not universal, but are significantly moderated by key factors, including intervention duration, teaching model and GenAI interaction method. (3) The findings identify potentially favourable instructional combinations for different learning objectives, such as enhancing academic or skill‐based outcomes. However, these subgroup results should be interpreted cautiously in relation to sample size, intervention duration and outcome measurement. These findings provide methodological guidance for university faculty to effectively integrate GenAI into classroom teaching and offer evidentiary support for policies aimed at enhancing teachers' AI instructional competency.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
Generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    and Learning Dynamics in Higher Education: A Longitudinal Empirical Study
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly integrated into higher education. Empirical evidence on how they shape learning dynamics over time remains limited. Previous studies have often examined single learning outcomes, neglecting the interplay between cognitive, motivational, and metacognitive processes that evolve throughout the semester.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This longitudinal study investigated how generative AI influences students' knowledge gain, motivation, cognitive load, critical thinking, and reflective use across an entire semester. It further explored whether prior knowledge and AI experience moderated these learning effects, addressing concerns about potential Matthew effects.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    
                      A quasi‐experimental design was implemented with three parallel classes of business informatics students (
                      N
                       = 87) assigned to different instructional conditions: tutor‐AI use, unguided AI, and a control group without AI. Data were collected at three measurement points (T1–T3).
                    
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusion
                    Students showed significant knowledge gains across all groups, but no additional benefits of AI integration. Motivation remained largely stable; germane cognitive load increased and was positively associated with knowledge gain. Critical thinking remained stable, while reflective use was higher in the AI condition and positively associated with critical thinking. No evidence emerged for a Matthew effect, indicating that AI did not intensify performance inequalities. Overall, the findings did not support the view of generative AI as a consistent learning outcome. Its impact depended on pedagogical framing and learners' metacognitive regulation, underscoring the need for structured guidance and reflective engagement in AI‐supported education.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
The Great Debaters Meet the Great Facilitators: How Debate Students Evaluate Human Moderators and Their
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Counterparts
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Debate cultivates reasoning, logic and persuasion, but its impact depends on skilled moderation, a role traditionally reserved for humans. Advances in large language models (LLMs) make Artificial Intelligence (AI) moderators a plausible alternative. Yet, little is known about how students perceive AI moderators compared to their human counterparts in educational debates.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study examines how university students evaluate human versus AI moderation in a synchronous, text‐based debate platform, focusing on moderation effectiveness, enjoyment, satisfaction, perceived utility and intention to use.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    
                      A quantitative experimental study was conducted using a synchronous text‐based debate platform. The study involved 32 university students from various universities in the United States who participated in 32 debate sessions. Each participant engaged in two debates moderated by human moderators, AI moderators or a combination of both across four moderator conditions: Human–Human, Bot–Bot, Human–Bot and Bot–Human. Following each debate, participants completed a questionnaire assessing moderation effectiveness, hedonic motivation, satisfaction, perceived utility and usage intention, resulting in a total of 64 observations. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, independent‐sample
                      t
                      ‐tests, multiple regression analyses and mediation analyses to examine differences between moderator types and the relationships among the study constructs. Ethical approval was obtained from the university's Research Ethics Committee, and informed consent was secured from all participants.
                    
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    Our analysis reveals no significant differences between human‐ and AI‐moderated debates across all measured dimensions. Across conditions, perceived effectiveness of moderation and hedonic motivation to use the platform predicted satisfaction and perceived utility. Perceived utility significantly drove usage intention, especially under AI moderation, whereas satisfaction more strongly predicted usage intention with human moderators. These findings suggest that, in well‐scaffolded, text‐based contexts with clear rules, thoughtfully designed AI moderators can match human facilitation while offering scalable support for equitable participation and structured discourse.

Education and Information Technologies.title: Design and validation of an integrated digital storytelling–problem-based learning system in primary mathematics: effects on conceptual understanding of decimal fractions
Education and Information Technologies.abstract:
Abstract
                  This study investigates the design and empirical validation of an integrated digital storytelling–problem-based learning (PBL) environment for supporting primary students’ conceptual understanding of decimal fractions. Decimal learning remains conceptually demanding due to students’ reliance on whole-number reasoning and difficulty coordinating symbolic and magnitude-based representations. Grounded in multimedia learning theory and inquiry-based pedagogy, the intervention operationalized digital storytelling as a structured multimodal construction process embedded within collaborative problem solving, positioning technology as a representational and cognitive regulation system rather than a presentation medium. A two-phase quasi-experimental nonequivalent control group design was implemented to evaluate both effectiveness and stability of the instructional model. Phase 1 included 66 Grade 5 students in one school, followed by a replication phase with 121 students across two additional schools to examine cross-context robustness. In both phases, posttest outcomes were analyzed using ANCOVA controlling for pretest performance. Assumptions of homogeneity of variances and regression slopes were satisfied. Results revealed a statistically significant effect of instructional condition in Phase 1, F(1, 62) = 5.38, p = .024, partial η² = .080, replicated in Phase 2, F(1, 117) = 6.19, p = .014, partial η² = .050. Students exposed to the integrated digital storytelling–PBL system demonstrated higher adjusted posttest scores than peers receiving traditional instruction. Pretest achievement remained a strong predictor of outcomes across phases. Findings indicate that when digital storytelling is systematically embedded within structured inquiry and aligned with multimedia learning principles, technology can operate as a coordinated instructional system supporting multimodal representational integration. Replication across independent samples strengthens confidence in the short-term stability of the model within authentic classroom environments. However, the quasi-experimental design, the use of intact classrooms, and the context-specific sample require cautious interpretation of causal claims and limit broad generalization.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Fostering Pre-Service Teachers’ Professional Problem Solving and Higher-Order Thinking Skills With a GenAI-Powered Interactive Fiction-Based Adaptive Teaching Simulation
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence offers substantial potential for teacher education programs; however, its passive or uncritical use may undermine higher-order thinking skills. Despite growing interest, empirical evidence on how GenAI can be pedagogically designed to actively foster professional cognition in pre-service teachers remains limited. Addressing this gap, the present study investigates the effects of a GenAI-powered Interactive Fiction–based Adaptive Teaching Simulation on pre-service teachers’ professional problem-solving skills and higher-order thinking skills. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, the present study involved 114 pre-service teachers, comprising a treatment group that engaged with the simulation and a control group that received non-simulation-based instruction. After controlling for pre-test scores, the treatment group obtained significantly higher post-test scores than the control group on the thinking and evaluator subdimensions of professional problem solving. Additionally, the treatment group showed higher adjusted post-test critical thinking scores than the control group, with a medium effect size. The qualitative findings supported these results, revealing that the system fostered reflective decision-making, multi-perspective reasoning, professional preparedness, and more informed and cautious perceptions regarding the use of GenAI in educational contexts. Overall, this study provides practical and theoretical implications for the pedagogically grounded integration of GenAI-powered Interactive Fiction simulations into teacher education programs.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: A Peer Assessment-Based Metaverse Inquiry Task Approach to Promoting Learning Achievement, Critical Thinking, Collaboration, and Creative Thinking: Evidence From Statistical and Epistemic Network Analysis
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
The metaverse provides new opportunities for designing learning activities in Information Systems (IS) education. This study integrated a pedagogical approach with the metaverse and examined its effectiveness on learning achievement, critical thinking awareness, collaborative tendencies, and creative thinking skills. A total of 50 university students (
                    M
                    
                      age
                    
                    =
                    19.4 years) participated in this quasi-experimental study. The experimental group engaged in a peer-assessment-based metaverse AICDR (Asking, Investigating, Creating, Discussing, and Reflecting) inquiry task (PA-MIT), while the control group followed a conventional metaverse AICDR inquiry task (C-MIT) over an 11-week intervention. Data were analyzed using ANCOVA to compare group differences in learning achievement, critical thinking awareness, and collaboration tendency, while epistemic network analysis (ENA) was applied to explore creative thinking patterns. Results showed that the PA-MIT group achieved significantly higher learning achievement and greater critical thinking awareness than the C-MIT group. However, no significant difference was found in collaboration tendencies. ENA further revealed stronger links among originality, flexibility, and fluency in the PA-MIT group, while the C-MIT group demonstrated strengths in elaboration, flexibility, and fluency. Results highlighted the role of the PA-MIT approach in fostering originality-oriented creative thinking. Peer feedback and idea exchange may lead to the interconnectedness of higher frequency originality-related discourse.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Differentiated Formative Feedback Through Parameterized ChatGPT: Effects on Knowledge Construction, Engagement, and Higher-Order Thinking in STEM Education
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: STEM education increasingly emphasizes interdisciplinary integration and self-directed learning, yet students with different achievement levels often face unequal challenges when navigating complex cross-domain content. High-achieving students may lack sufficient cognitive stimulation, whereas low-achieving students may struggle with overwhelming complexity. Standard ChatGPT feedback lacks adaptability to these diverse learner capabilities, leaving some students unchallenged and others overloaded. Addressing these disparities requires timely and differentiated instructional support. This study proposes AdjustGPT, a system that calibrates ChatGPT’s generative parameters (temperature, max_tokens, frequency_penalty, presence_penalty, and top_p) according to learners’ achievement levels to deliver differentiated formative feedback. Grounded in formative feedback theory and cognitive load principles, AdjustGPT provides high-achieving students with exploratory, multi-perspective feedback that fosters critical thinking and innovation, while offering low-achieving students clear, structured guidance that reduces cognitive load and strengthens foundational understanding. A quasi-experimental study with 62 university students in a STEM course showed that, within this exploratory sample, AdjustGPT was associated with significant gains in knowledge construction, cognitive and emotional engagement, and higher-order thinking outcomes, including critical thinking and problem-solving. These findings provide initial evidence that parameterized ChatGPT systems can support adaptive formative feedback and differentiated AI-assisted teaching in STEM education. Larger-scale studies are needed to establish robustness and generalizability.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: The Applications and Roles of Generative Artificial Intelligence in School-Aged Student Creativity Development: A Systematic Review
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly entered creativity-oriented education since 2022, yet evidence on its applications and roles in school-aged student creativity development (SCD) remains fragmented. This systematic review addresses two questions: (1) What architectures, tools, and modalities of GenAI support SCD? and (2) What facilitating and constraining roles do GenAI primarily play across creativity dimensions, and what inter-role dynamics emerge among them? Following PRISMA 2020, we searched five databases and two supplementary sources, identifying 57 empirical studies published between 2022 and 2026. Descriptive analysis mapped GenAI architectures, modalities and tools, while inductive–deductive coding synthesised GenAI roles using Rhodes’s 4 Ps creativity framework. Results revealed that GenAI tools built on transformer-based large language models and diffusion models and operating through text-to-text and text-to-image modalities dominated applications. Regarding GenAI’s roles in SCD, we identified 20 distinct roles, 19 of which were distributed across 4 Ps, and revealed three dynamic inter-role patterns. This study adds a new insight to Rhodes’s 4 Ps by incorporating the role of Co-Creator as a fifth P, Partnership, to capture the proactive, dialogic, and distributed nature of human-machine co-creation. Implications are discussed for “role-aware” tool selection, pedagogy, and future research on underrepresented modalities and partnership dynamics.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Metaverse-Based Self-Regulated Learning in Nursing Dietary Education: Effects on Learning Achievement, Self-Efficacy, Critical Thinking Awareness, and Behavioral Patterns
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: A central goal of foundational dietary education is to enhance nursing students’ learning achievement, self-efficacy, and critical thinking awareness. However, providing personalized guidance in conventional instructional settings remains challenging. To address these limitations, the present study introduces a structured metaverse-based self-regulated learning framework designed to promote personalized, immersive, and contextually rich learning experiences in dietary education. A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 44 undergraduate nursing students enrolled in an introductory course on cancer-preventive dietary practices. Participants were assigned to either a metaverse-based self-regulated learning condition (experimental group) or a conventional 2D video-based instruction condition (control group). Findings indicate that students in the metaverse-based condition demonstrated significantly higher levels of learning achievement, self-efficacy, and critical thinking awareness than peers in the conventional instruction group. Exploratory behavioral analyses of the 22 experimental-group participants, categorized by a median split, suggested that learners with higher critical thinking awareness exhibited more structured, reflective, and proactive learning patterns, whereas those with lower awareness relied more on feedback-dependent strategies. Overall, metaverse-based self-regulated learning enhanced learning achievement, self-efficacy, and critical thinking awareness, while providing preliminary insights into learners’ behavioral patterns in nursing education.

Early Childhood Education Journal.title: Building a Strong Math Foundation: Supporting Early Math Precursors for Babies and Toddlers
Early Childhood Education Journal.abstract:
Abstract
                  Research is finding that exposure to early math during the baby and toddler stages is valuable for their later mathematical outcomes; however, what this looks like in practice has had relatively limited exploration. In response, this study provides insight into the presence of early math precursors (foundational pre-mathematical skills such as attribute, comparison, change, patterns), as detailed by Hynes-Berry, Chen, & Abel, in six public library storytimes for babies and toddlers. This qualitative descriptive study consisted of naturalistic observations and deductive and inductive coding of video-recorded storytimes. Participants included six library educators, 63 babies and toddlers, and 61 caregivers. The observations revealed that all four early math precursors are present in the storytimes through a variety of methods, strategies, and resources the educators and caregivers used with the babies and toddlers. Through the lens of Bruner’s Three Modes of Representation and Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development, findings offer insight into how library and other early childhood educators can better support the precursors through embodied learning, manipulatives, vocabulary, and other developmentally-appropriate supports for babies and toddlers. Additionally, by operationalizing a coding schema using Hynes-Berry et al.’s work, this study also helps to advance a methodological approach for identifying early math precursors in early childhood settings.

Early Childhood Education Journal.title: Examining Influence on Early Care and Education Teachers’ Intention to Leave: Compensation, Workplace Support, and Depressive Symptoms
Early Childhood Education Journal.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    High turnover among early care and education (ECE) teachers threatens workforce stability and may have negative implications for ECE program quality and children’s early learning and development. Previous research limited to specific regions or small samples has linked low compensation, workplace support, and mental well-being to teacher’ turnover intentions. However, these associations have not yet been examined within nationally representative data. This preregistered study examined the extent to which compensation, workplace support, and depressive symptoms were associated with turnover intention among a nationally representative sample of center-based ECE teachers. It also explore whether depressive symptoms moderated the links between compensation and workplace support and turnover intention. The study relied on data from the 2019 National Survey of Early Care and Education (NSECE) Workforce Questionnaire (
                    N
                     = 3,379). Weighted binary logistic regression analyses were conducted, as well as tests of two interaction effects between depressive symptoms and workplace support and between depressive symptoms and hourly wage. Results demonstrated that greater workplace support was associated with lower odds of turnover intention, and more depressive symptoms was associated with greater odds of turnover intention. Hourly wage was not significantly associated with turnover intention. Moreover, we did not find evidence of depressive symptoms moderating the associations between workplace support or hourly wage and turnover intention. Ultimately, the findings from this study suggest that workplace support and mental well-being may be particularly important to target to improve retention in the ECE workforce.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Reimagining Froebelian principles to engage and support low-income families in early childhood policy
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: This paper makes three important contributions to the early years field in England. First, it highlights the barriers to play experienced by low-income families. Second, it illuminates parents’ affinity with Froebelian principles without prior knowledge of them. Third, it suggests how these affinities could be taken up in early years policy. This paper draws on previous research which revealed that many early years’ practitioners believe low-income families often do not value play. In so doing, it presents findings from our recent study which invited low-income families to reflect on and explore the potential of applying Froebel’s ideas in their interactions with their child(ren) during play. Through interviews, families shared their experiences, perceptions, and understandings of Froebelian approaches to play. Notably, parents engaged with Froebelian concepts in practice, even though they did not explicitly identify or label them as such. The findings suggest a need to adapt and extend Froebelian principles to be more inclusive and accessible to low-income families. This research offers valuable insights for practitioners by providing empirical evidence of diverse parental perspectives on play, highlighting opportunities to learn from families and support play-based learning at home. It also holds implications for policy, identifying areas where changes are needed to address the impact of socio-economic disadvantage on families with young children.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Organizational culture in leading pedagogical work in Finnish early childhood education: A discourse analysis
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Finnish early childhood education has undergone many changes over the past decade. These changes have strengthened the position of Early Childhood Education (ECE) within the education system. ECE teachers are now responsible for planning the activities for groups of children, implementation of activities with a goal-oriented and systematic approach and evaluating and developing the activities. ECE teachers are responsible for leading the pedagogical activities of the multiprofessional team; however the leadership role of teachers remains unclear. This study examines how organizational culture is constructed in discourses on leading pedagogical work in Finnish ECE. The theoretical framework is based on the concepts of pedagogical leadership, distributed pedagogical leadership, teacher leadership, and organizational culture. The data consist of interviews with 11 ECE teachers. We analysed the data using discourse analysis as a method. We identified four discourses in the data: the discourse of varied clarity, the discourse of balancing act, the discourse of competition, and the discourse of varied support. Considering this study, there are varying organizational cultural prerequisites for leading a team’s pedagogical activities in Finnish ECE. The results can help to understand the phenomenon of teacher leadership. The results can also help centre directors develop the organization’s culture so that it better supports teachers in their leadership task.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Educators’ perspectives on early language facilitation with children aged birth to 2 years in early childhood education and care in Finland
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: The first two years of life are critical for later language learning and performance. With an increasing number of children participating in institutional early childhood education and care (ECEC), this has become an important language learning environment. ECEC educators play a key role in facilitating children’s language development and hence their views on the possibilities and constraints for facilitating young children’s language in ECEC are valuable. The study presented in this paper, explored educators’ views on aspects linked to early language facilitation in ECEC with children aged birth to two years. A large-scale semi-structured survey related to early language facilitation in ECEC was completed by 644 educators. Their open-ended responses were analysed using qualitative inductive content analysis. Factors constraining and facilitating language development in ECEC were extracted from the data and grouped into four categories: characteristics of educators as prerequisites for language facilitation; daily group practices in ECEC; ECEC service policy and resources; and ECEC in the context of wider societal and family services. While many existing well-functioning practices for early language facilitation were noted, challenges were also reported. In addition to employing skilled staff, educators saw it as important to organise practices and daily routines in ways that support language facilitation. They also emphasised that setting lower educator-child ratios and taking children’s skills and age into account when forming groups would create more frequent language-facilitation situations involving educator-child reciprocal communications. Overall, the educators perceived ECEC as a low-threshold service for early language intervention. They considered language facilitation for young children to be essential and to require multi-professional cooperation and resources.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: “I like to play with my Grandfriends”: Participants’ experiences in a co-located intergenerational program
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Research on intergenerational programs (IGPs) has documented cognitive, physical and social outcomes for older adults, and beneficial effects for children such as enhanced empathy and more positive attitudes toward older adults. However, there is a relative scarcity of research documenting the benefits of co-located intergenerational programs, whereby the aged-care facility and early learning program are housed under the same roof, thus offering opportunities for frequent intergenerational connections across structured and unstructured activities. Moreover, research providing a consolidated account of the benefits of participation from the perspectives of multiple participant groups, especially young children, is limited. As such, this qualitative case study explores the perspectives of multiple participants engaged in a co-located aged-care facility and early learning centre in Melbourne, Australia: 19 young children and their families, seven early learning and aged-care staff, and seven older adults. The methodology involved semi-structured interviews conducted with staff, online surveys completed by families, and draw, write, and tell method to elicit children’s perspectives. The analysis was framed by social capital theory which pays attention to the relationships within and between groups (bonding and bridging), and the associated benefits for individual and group capabilities. Thematic analysis of the qualitative data revealed two overarching themes – “Program design and implementation” and “Impact for participants” – comprising five categories which highlight the importance of relational factors to nurture mutually beneficial bridging and bonding relationships, and structural program elements such as collaborative planning to support optimal outcomes for all participants.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Children’s use of symbolic “anchors”: Color and shape in map-making activities
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: This research study focuses on children’s symbolic development, especially looking at color and shape as symbolic anchors in children’s expressive communication. Framed by Vygotsky’s cognitive development theory, which includes the roles of social interaction, cultural tools, and the zone of proximal development (ZPD), as well as Mead’s social interactionism, the study was designed as mixed-methods research with data collection from children’s map artifacts, map-making video recording and audio transcriptions, and a data collection matrix. By tracking the performance of 10 children (n/x = 10) in creating maps for 2 years, when they were approximately 4 years old (year 1, mean age = 52.5 months), and in Pre-K (year 2, mean age = 71 months), when they were approximately 5 years old, we examined children’s symbol use. It was observed that exposure to and engagement with relational language promotes children’s analogical reasoning. We also found that the children’s use of symbols, and especially symbolic anchors, increased overtime, demonstrating expanded perspective-taking ability. Lastly, it is our observation that children’s use of shape as a symbolic anchor seems to appear prior to children’s use of color in the emergence of symbolic representation.

keyword_papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Early Childhood STEM Education: A Review of Pedagogical Paradigms, Ethical Issues, and Socio-Political Implications
keyword_papers.abstract: This study examines the pedagogical, ethical, and political dimensions of artificial intelligence (AI) in early childhood STEM education from a theoretical perspective. As digital technologies become increasingly prevalent in education, AI applications offer significant opportunities in areas such as personalized learning experiences, game-based education, and data analytics. However, they also pose critical ethical concerns, including data security, algorithmic bias, and privacy, while influencing children's cognitive, linguistic, and social development. Drawing on Piaget’s theory of active discovery and learning, Vygotsky’s emphasis on social interaction and teacher guidance, and Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems theory, this study explores how AI-supported learning environments can enrich children's natural developmental processes. A qualitative literature review and theoretical analysis reveal the necessity of achieving a balanced integration between the individualized educational opportunities offered by AI and the potential risks it entails. The findings highlight the critical importance of developing human-centered, ethically sound, and inclusive educational models for educators, policymakers, and researchers in the face of technological transformation. In this context, teacher training, parental collaboration, and interdisciplinary strategies are identified as fundamental prerequisites for the sustainable and effective integration of AI in early childhood education.
keyword_papers.venue: Journal of Education in Science Environment and Health

keyword_papers.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Early Childhood Education
keyword_papers.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into early childhood education presents new opportunities and challenges in fostering cognitive, social, and emotional development. This theoretical discussion synthesizes recent research on AI’s role in personalized learning, educational robotics, gamified learning, and social-emotional development. The study explores theoretical frameworks such as Vygotsky’s Sociocultural Theory, Distributed Cognition, and the Five Big Ideas Framework to understand AI’s impact on young learners. AI-powered personalized learning platforms enhance engagement and adaptability, while robotics and gamification foster problem-solving and collaboration. Additionally, AI tools support children with disabilities, promoting inclusivity and accessibility. However, ethical concerns related to privacy, bias, and teacher preparedness pose challenges to effective AI integration. Furthermore, the long-term effects of AI on children’s social skills and emotional intelligence require further investigation. This theoretical discussion emphasizes the need for interdisciplinary collaboration to develop AI-driven educational strategies that prioritize developmental appropriateness, equity, and ethical considerations. The findings highlight AI’s potential as a transformative educational tool, provided it is implemented thoughtfully and responsibly. The paper aims to address the following research question: How can artificial intelligence (AI) be meaningfully and ethically integrated into early childhood education to enhance learning, while preserving developmental and relational values?

keyword_papers.title: A new era in early childhood education (ECE): Teachers’ opinions on the application of artificial intelligence
keyword_papers.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the role of AI in preschool from the perspective of preschool teachers. The research group consisted of 101 preschool teachers. The study group was selected according to the easily accessible case sampling method, one of the purposeful sampling methods. The study was a phenomenology, which is a qualitative research design. Qualitative data were collected using a semi-structured interview form. Data were analyzed using inductive content analysis. As a result of the analyses, the participants stated they did not feel sufficient regarding Al literacy and competencies. The participants also emphasized that using AI in preschool was appropriate and would improve children’s skills, such as AI literacy and computational thinking. Moreover, they stated that using AI in preschool would cause privacy and security concerns for different reasons, such as not protecting personal data, using children’s pictures, and providing false and misleading information. The participants stated that they were worried about the implementation process of Al due to lack of content knowledge, lack of infrastructure, physical structure of the classroom, and lack of materials. In addition, participants emphasized that if the existing concerns were eliminated, AI could be easily integrated into the preschool period. In addition, it was determined that most participants had problems in modeling and drawing a model related to AI.
keyword_papers.venue: Education and Information Technologies : Official Journal of the IFIP technical committee on Education

keyword_papers.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Driven Curriculum Development in Early Childhood Education: Educators' Insights, Barriers, and Policy Pathways
keyword_papers.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in early childhood education (ECE) has gained global attention for its potential to enhance personalized learning and inclusivity. However, challenges such as teacher preparedness, infrastructure limitations, and ethical concerns hinder its effective implementation, particularly in developing contexts. This study explores the perceptions of educators regarding AI-driven curriculum development in ECE, identifies challenges and opportunities, and assesses the effectiveness of AI-based learning models. A qualitative research approach was used, involving semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions with 20 educators from two districts of Lahore, Pakistan. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings indicate that AI enhances engagement, supports personalized learning, and benefits children with special needs. However, infrastructure gaps and lack of teacher training remain major barriers. The study recommends capacity-building programs for educators, policy frameworks for ethical AI adoption, and investment in digital infrastructure to ensure equitable access to AI-driven education.

keyword_papers.title: From Turing’s conception of machine intelligence to the evolution of AI in early childhood education: conceptual, empirical, and practical insights
keyword_papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly permeating many aspects of our everyday lives and nearly every sector of society. In education, AI innovations are increasingly recognized for their transformative potential for enhancing teaching and student learning. In this article, I focus specifically on the evolution of AI in early childhood education (ECE), serving children from birth to age 8. To shed light on this phenomenon, I synthesize pertinent literature to yield conceptual, empirical, and practical insights. I begin with a historical perspective, tracing the origins of Turing’s conception of machine intelligence and the term “AI” to the current practical applications of AI in ECE and AI use by, for, and with children. I then examine developmental appropriateness and ethical considerations surrounding AI use. Next, I identify new opportunities and challenges for early childhood teachers, offering practical recommendations for education leaders and proposing future research directions. Finally, I conclude by reimagining an AI-powered future of ECE, emphasizing the need for supportive practices, active engagement, and the cultivation of positive dispositions among all key stakeholders, who must keep pace with the evolving AI landscape by navigating new opportunities, emerging challenges, and innovative developments. Additionally, I reimagine a transformative educational landscape enriched by student-centered, innovative teaching practices that catalyze learning in an AI-child interactive environment. In this reimagined and progressive educational landscape, the children are empowered with equal opportunities and equitable resources to naturally learn about and from developmentally appropriate AI tools as well as leverage them in ethical and responsible ways to enhance their learning.

keyword_papers.title: Developmentally aligned AI: a framework for translating the science of child development into AI design
keyword_papers.abstract: What would it mean to design AI not for the average user, but for the child whose fingers still miss the screen, who forgets the instructions halfway through, and who greets the voice in the box as a friend? This paper proposes Developmentally Aligned Design (DAD) as a practical and ethical framework for building AI systems that meet children where they are—cognitively, socially, and emotionally. Building on the long-standing principle of developmentally appropriate practice in early childhood education, it theorises four principles of developmentally-aligned design: (1) perceptual fit (e.g., anonymised phoneme‑error tuning in early‑reading apps that respects toddlers’ speech‑production limits) (2) cognitive scaffolding (e.g. Zone‑of‑Proximal‑Development (ZPD) progressions that govern when a tutoring agent introduces harder tasks) (3) interface simplicity (e.g., storybook apps that cap menu depth and visual clutter to match preschoolers’ working‑memory span) and (4) relational integrity (e.g., conversational agents that introduce themselves with a developmentally clear disclaimer—“I’m a computer helper, not a real friend”). Through illustrative examples, it demonstrates how developmental science can serve as a validation layer on AI dataset curation, model fine‑tuning, and user experience choices. Adopting Developmentally Aligned Design can therefore sensitise AI systems to the distinct perceptual, cognitive, and socio‑emotional needs of young children; shift the responsibility of “proof of safety” from parents and early‑years practitioners to AI developers and vendors; and help the science of child development become a core intellectual engine of next‑generation AI innovation.

keyword_papers.title: The Future of Child Development in the AI Era. Cross-Disciplinary Perspectives Between AI and Child Development Experts
keyword_papers.abstract: This report explores the potential implications of rapidly integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications into children's environments. The introduction of AI in our daily lives necessitates scrutiny considering the significant role of the environment in shaping cognition, socio-emotional skills, and behaviors, especially during the first 25 years of cerebral development. As AI becomes prevalent in educational and leisure activities, it will significantly modify the experiences of children and adolescents, presenting both challenges and opportunities for their developmental trajectories. This analysis was informed by consulting with 15 experts from pertinent disciplines (AI, product development, child development, and neurosciences), along with a comprehensive review of scientific literature on children development and child-technology interactions. Overall, AI experts anticipate that AI will transform leisure activities, revolutionize education, and redefine human-machine interactions. While AI offers substantial benefits in fostering interactive engagement, it also poses risks that require careful considerations, especially during sensitive developmental periods. The report advocates for proactive international collaboration across multiple disciplines and increased research into how technological innovations affect child development. Such efforts are crucial for designing a sustainable and ethical future for the next generation through specific child-centered regulations, and helping to educate all potential stakeholders (regulators, developers, parents and educators, children) about responsible AI use and its potential impacts on child development.

keyword_papers.title: AI, Brain, and Child: navigating the intersection of artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and child development
keyword_papers.abstract: In an era marked by rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and cognitive neuroscience, the intersection of these fields holds transformative potential for child development and educational practices. This launch editorial introduces AI, Brain and Child (ABC), an open-access journal dedicated to exploring the dynamic interplay between AI, neuroscience, and child education. By fostering an interdisciplinary dialogue among educators, researchers, clinicians, and policymakers, ABC aims to examine the multifaceted roles of AI and neuroscience in shaping cognitive, social, and emotional growth among children. The journal seeks to democratize access to high-quality research, addressing both the beneficial applications and ethical challenges posed by AI and neuroscience technologies. Through this platform, ABC aspires to promote evidence-based practices, enhance educational outcomes, and tackle pressing developmental and educational issues. By welcoming diverse contributions—from empirical research to policy analysis—ABC endeavors to bridge the gaps between theory and practice, equipping stakeholders with the insights needed to navigate the complexities of educating children within a technologically enriched landscape. This new scholarly endeavor marks a new era of global community to partake in the crucial conversation surrounding the opportunities and responsibilities inherent in integrating AI and neuroscience into education.

keyword_papers.title: AI-Driven Design of Emotionally Supportive Toys for Child Development: An Iterative Process
keyword_papers.abstract: Background Emotional support is critical for children's social skills and well-being. Children exposed to emotional support at an early age can foster resilience and interpersonal skills. As traditional support methods lack interactive and personalized engagement, innovative, technology-driven solutions are consequently developed. Objective This project aimed to develop an AI-driven “emotional mentor” embodied in a plush bear whose inherent characteristic is comfort and companionship. The goal was to create a visually appealing and emotionally supportive tool that encourages children to recognize and express their feelings through gentle interaction. The design specifically targets children aged 3-11, a critical period of emotional development defined by Freudian psychology. Method The project utilized AI visual generation models guided by precise prompts, following a systematic, iterative design process. Initial design concepts were generated by AI visual generation models with precise prompts. Early outputs were critically evaluated for inconsistencies, excessive detail, and unwanted features. After iterative updates, the prompts can finally output simplicity, warmth, and an inviting appearance. LoRA fine-tuning was used to balance function and aesthetics. Market research informed the incorporation of subtle “breathing” motion effects, and user perception testing also informed the design. Results The iterative design process yielded a prototype of an emotionally supportive plush toy with refined visual aesthetics and glowing interactive features. The AI-assisted design facilitated the exploration of a range of design concepts and the systematic improvement of the toy's visual and interactive elements. Conclusion This study presents a detailed, AI-assisted iterative approach to designing an emotionally supportive plush toy. The design process and interactive visual features are the core. Future work may explore additional functionalities to further enhance the system's emotional support capabilities.

keyword_papers.title: AI, Parenting, and Child Development.
keyword_papers.abstract: Abstract not available.
